title: Daisy reports permissions as missing when they are already granted
description:
What happens On launch, Daisy shows Accessibility and Input Monitoring as missing and will not start the listener, even though Daisy is already switched on in System Settings → Privacy & Security. Requesting again does nothing. The only way out is to remove Daisy from both lists and grant it again, or re-add the app by hand. Likely cause macOS ties these permissions to the app's code signature, not its name. A build signed differently (for example a local Apple Development build versus the Developer ID release, or an older build) shows up as "Daisy" in System Settings but does not count for the running app. Daisy then sees no permission and blocks Start. Expected - Daisy does not refuse to start on a pre-check that can be wrong; it starts and reports what actually fails.
- When a permission is missing but Daisy appears in the list, Daisy says the entry belongs to another copy and offers to fix it (remove and re-add), instead of looping on requests.
- Input Monitoring granted while Daisy is running is picked up, with a relaunch if macOS requires one. Affected Daisy 0.1.0 and 0.1.1.
acceptance_criteria: Daisy starts with valid permissions on a clean install and after an upgrade from 0.1.1; a stale entry from another signature is detected and explained with a fix; no remove-and-re-add loop. Verified on hardware with the release build.
notes: GitHub: https://github.com/misfitdev/daisy/issues/6

title: Device-bound identity: trust a system's hardware, not a portable key file
description: Each system's identity is a key file (~/Library/Application Support/daisy/identity). A copy is that system: backups, Migration Assistant and anything running as the user can carry it to another machine, which then connects as the original. A system's identity must not be forgeable, impersonable or portable.
design: Secure Enclave P-256 key per system (non-exportable, not in backups or migration). Peers pin its public key at pairing beside the Noise static key. Every session: each side signs the Noise handshake hash with its Secure Enclave key; the other verifies against the pinned key, so a copied Noise key alone cannot connect. Introductions and revocations signed by the Secure Enclave key. Limits: malware on the device itself can still request signatures (Touch ID per signature would close that but breaks unattended reconnect). Verify first: Secure Enclave key creation in a Developer ID build may need keychain-access-groups/application-identifier entitlements and a provisioning profile. Protocol change: new handshake step, so a protocol VERSION bump.
acceptance_criteria: Copied Noise identity on another system cannot reconnect without the pinned Secure Enclave signature. Device identity keys are non-exportable Secure Enclave P-256 keys persisted in the Data Protection Keychain with no user-presence prompts. Protocol 5 and fresh trust state are a hard cut: existing groups pair again, with no identity or trust conversion. Introductions and revocations use the device key. Tests reject missing, wrong, replayed and reflected device signatures.
notes:
Decision: no user-presence access control; reconnect signing stays silent. Implemented Secure Enclave P-256 keys in the Data Protection Keychain, restricted to this system, with a lookup reference on disk. Protocol 5 signs the Noise handshake hash and sender role before trust negotiation; pairing atomically pins Noise and device keys. Introductions and revocations use the same device key. Hard cut to fresh trust-v5 state, with no conversion of earlier groups. Device-key rotation deletes the previous Keychain key. Signed bundle preparation validates and embeds a matching provisioning profile; release CI expects DEVELOPER_ID_PROFILE_BASE64. Validation: just check passed (336 library tests, 3 ignored, plus CLI/menu/doc gates); cargo audit, cargo deny, ReachSec, zizmor and actionlint passed; site build passed. Reflection and copied-Noise-identity rejection tests were demonstrated failing with their protections removed, then restored. Developer ID signed checks on the local system, macOS 27.2, confirmed key creation, signing/verification, Keychain persistence across processes, denied private export, and rejection of the obsolete reference after rotation. Temporary test keys were removed. Two-system hardware testing was not run. ReachSec revision 548b228ba35774664d4d691b6fddf537aa6225db. No Git commit, push, or Dolt synchronization performed.
Completed required trust prerequisite for file transfer. File transfer, and therefore device-bound identity trust, is the 1.0.0 release gate; this work alone does not complete that gate.

title: Signed introductions and revocations
description: Joining a group pairs with one member, who introduces the newcomer to the rest. Add a long-term Ed25519 signing key (identity file migrates from the 64-byte X25519 format; rotate-key rotates both). The introducer signs the newcomer's keys, name, policy and expiry; members accept it because they trust the introducer, and record introduced_by in peers.toml (serde defaults for old files). Introduced trust never outlives the introducer's and is never looser. Signed revocations propagate to every member; forgetting a system also revokes everything it introduced. Rewrite docs/security-model.md: a compromised member can admit a new system. Codes stay PAKE input only.
acceptance_criteria: Tests: an introduction verifies only with the introducer's key and binds the newcomer's keys; an expired or tampered introduction is refused; revocation removes the system and its introductions everywhere; introduced trust is bounded by the introducer's; old identity and peer files load.

Members introduce every trusted system with signed introductions at link start and when pairing; receivers accept only from the named introducer with its pinned key, under the stricter policy, cascading with the introducer. Forgetting signs a revocation that removes the system and what it introduced group-wide; stale introductions cannot undo it. Security model updated.

title: Route the pointer to any screen in the group
description: Input::Driver crosses through one Side of one bounding Rect and Target only leaves back toward the driver. With the group layout (mn-pu5.1), the driver decides where the pointer goes: Enter carries the entry point in the target's coordinates; Target reports Leave with its exit point and direction on any outside edge; the driver then routes to the next system by direction of travel within reach, which may be a third system or back home. Edges between one system's own displays never cross. Replaces Along and Side in Enter/Leave (protocol 3, unreleased).
acceptance_criteria: Pure tests over three-system layouts: chains A->B->C and back, corners, gaps within reach, no crossing between a system's own displays, no route into an overlap (impossible by construction).
close_reason: Crossings carry a destination and an exact point. Every system knows every member's displays and one agreed arrangement (greatest version wins); the system being driven hands the pointer on to a third system or home. Its remaining dependency on mn-pu5.1 is that issue's UI and display-change work, tracked there.

title: One owner of control across the group
description: control::Control models two systems: owner is a bool, generations are per link, ties break on the Noise initiator, and receives() ignores the sender. Make ownership group-wide: claims carry (generation, claimant key), are sent on every link, and order totally by generation then key. Each system knows the current driver; it injects only input stamped by that driver at that generation and releases held input when the owner changes. The clipboard goes from the system giving up control to the one taking it. A link that drops while its peer drives returns control locally.
acceptance_criteria: Pure tests: simultaneous claims from three systems converge on one owner without flapping; input from a non-owner or an older generation is dropped; held input is released on every change; the chord recovers locally on any member.
close_reason: Control is owned by one named system across the group: claims carry generation and claimant, order by (generation, key), ControlState on join, only the owner is played, losing the owner takes control back.

title: Run a session with every group member at once
description: Today one session runs per process: service::automatic, listen and connect await a whole session before accepting, dialing or advertising again, and run_session builds its own SharedControl, Capture (event tap) and Injector. Split this into one process-wide input core (one tap, one injector, one control state, one replay Target, clipboard Sharing) and one link actor per peer (Channel, Incoming/Outgoing, heartbeat, Silent, latency Meter, peers.watch, Visit). Keep advertising and browsing while connected; connect to every trusted member found, using discovery::opens_connection per pair; accept connections concurrently. Cap the group at 8 systems. The observer reports per peer, and the controller keeps a set of links instead of one Status::Connected.
acceptance_criteria: Two or more links run at once in tests with fake peers; a link dropping leaves the others running; the 9th system is refused with a clear reason; one event tap per process.
notes: 2026-10-01: core done (share::run with links, service Hub, concurrent automatic/listen). Remaining for the status UI is in mn-pu5.6: the controller still shows one peer; ControllerObserver::disconnected switches to waiting even while other links remain.

title: Arrange every display of every system, like Displays
description: Daisy treats all of a system's displays as one bounding rectangle and places the peer against one side of it. Replace that with per-display geometry: each system sends its display rectangles (points, relative to its main display) and re-sends on change. The peer's displays move as one group, placed by an offset instead of a Side. Placement is free (gaps and corner-only contact allowed) but never overlaps: dragging stops at an edge and slides along it, a drop settles at the nearest clear spot, and a display change that makes the saved placement overlap moves the group the shortest clearing distance. Light snap within about 8 points, with Option held to skip it. Crossing: leaving an outside edge continues in the direction of travel into the first peer display within a reach of about 40 points (edges, small gaps, corner chains). Entry is on that display's edge and leaving mirrors it; edges between a system's own displays never cross. The receiving pointer is kept on real displays, not the bounding box. Protocol: a displays message, an offset in Layout, exact points in Enter/Leave; ships in protocol 3 with no further bump (unreleased). The window draws all displays at true relative size, the peer group drags as one, the coral highlight marks the display holding the pointer, and edge stretches that cross are highlighted. Stored Sides convert to offsets. The geometry (outlines, no-overlap check, snapping, crossing lookup, mapping) is a pure, unit-tested module. With many peers the no-overlap rule applies between every pair of systems.
acceptance_criteria: A laptop with an external monitor can place the peer along any outside edge of either display without overlap. Crossing works from each such edge and never between local displays. Plugging or unplugging a display mid-session re-validates the placement. Geometry decisions are unit tested.
notes: 2026-10-01: geometry (src/layout.rs) and the agreed arrangement (Placement, Displays/Arrangement messages) are done and used for routing. Remaining: re-send Displays when a display is plugged, removed or rearranged; persist offsets across restarts (today a peer is placed from its stored side when it joins); the window drawing every member's displays with the peer's group draggable, snapping and Option to skip.

title: Diagnose severe input lag after reconnecting
description: Inspect the live running Daisy session during reported mouse and keyboard lag after reconnecting. Preserve process samples and network evidence without stopping or restarting Daisy. Identify the bottleneck and make any justified fix reviewable.
notes:
Live diagnosis on the local system (macOS 27.2), installed Daisy PID 65824, left running. User reproduced approximately two-second pauses during a held key in either forwarding direction; local keyboard into the same local input box is smooth. TCP captures: smoothed RTT approximately 9.6–17.7 ms; retransmission/duplicate counters flat during measured intervals; no sustained receive backlog (1500 observations over 17.8 seconds, 4 nonzero receive observations, max 26 bytes; send max 42 bytes). Daisy event tap average approximately 0.13–0.33 ms, observed maximum approximately 18.3 ms. Process profiles showed background workers mostly waiting and input injection active, without a sustained local stall. Main thread is inside an old modal connection-error alert, confirmed through native UI; local permission polling was not firing in these samples. Another system keyboard filter reported high timing values, but its profile did not establish a causal stall. Wi-Fi logs show AWDL channel scheduling and a prior scan; no event-level correlation yet. Packet capture and WindowServer sampling require administrator access unavailable to this session. Peer remote access is disabled by policy: do not retry or enable it. Root cause remains unconfirmed. Next evidence: a process sample taken locally on the peer while reproducing, or an administrator-run header-only packet timing capture on the local system. Evidence is preserved in /tmp/daisy-live-sample.txt, /tmp/daisy-live-key-repeat-sample.txt, /tmp/daisy-live-network.csv, /tmp/daisy-live-key-repeat-network.csv, /tmp/daisy-live-bidirectional-network.csv, /tmp/daisy-live-taps.json, and /tmp/daisy-live-socket-queues.csv. No source changes or restart in this investigation.
Follow-up: user confirmed the approximately two-second pause persists after dismissing the blocking modal alert; Daisy remained running. Audited application intervals, tick counters, blocking timed waits, and mdns-sd/backon runtime scheduling. No third fixed two-second loop found. Additional timers: live peer trust checks every second, renewals every 20 seconds, Bonjour IP checks every five seconds, and exponentially spaced Bonjour queries (including a transient two-second delay). title: Control follows whichever Mac you are using
description:
## Summary

Remove Host/Guest and Wait/Connect from the interface. Whichever Mac has hands on its keyboard or trackpad drives; the other follows. Moving to the other Mac and using it hands control over automatically, and the screen arrangement stays the same, because the layout is stored as one relation both Macs share ("A's right edge meets B") rather than as per-Mac roles.

## Behavior

- Both Macs watch their own input at all times. Physical input (not input Daisy posted) on a Mac makes it the driver: it sends a claim, the other Mac releases what it holds and follows.
- Local input always wins: touching a Mac's own keyboard or trackpad returns control to it immediately.
- A short settle window prevents control flapping when both Macs are used at once.
- Setup is: pair, then say which side the other Mac sits on. Status names the other Mac ("Connected to …"), not roles.
- With Bonjour, both Macs advertise and the pair agrees deterministically who opens the connection; Wait for a peer / Connect by Address leave the default UI (typing an address stays available for networks Bonjour does not reach).

## Consequences

- Every Mac needs both Accessibility and Input Monitoring; the role-aware permission rule from #11 is simplified.
- Protocol: messages to claim control and to agree on the shared layout (appended variants).
- Swipe capture still requires macOS 27 on the Mac in use.

Using either Mac's keyboard or trackpad makes it the driver within one event, with the arrangement unchanged; local input always wins; no flapping with brief simultaneous use. title: Per-Mac trust policies and forced revocation
description:
Trust is forever today: a Mac paired once, long ago, can connect and take   
over the keyboard at any time. Make trust a policy chosen per Mac, expiring 
by default.                                                                 
                                                                            
Policies:                                                                   
                                                                            
• Idle limit, the default: trust ends after 96 hours without an             
authenticated session with that Mac. Refreshed while connected, at least    
every heartbeat interval, so a pair that stays connected never expires.     
• For N days: a hard deadline N days after pairing, however often the Macs  
connect. Being connected does not extend it.                                
• Just this once: the key is kept in memory only and trust ends with the    
session. After an unexpected drop, the same key may reconnect without a code
for 60 seconds; after a deliberate disconnect, never.                       
• Forever: never expires until forgotten. Always shown as such, since it is 
the one that brings back the original risk.                                 
                                                                            
Rules:                                                                      
                                                                            
• Each Mac enforces its own policy for the other, with its own clock. Trust 
needs both sides, so the stricter policy wins and a peer cannot override    
this Mac's choice by claiming it still trusts us.                           
• Expired trust means unpaired: refuse the Mac, drop its stored key, and    
require pairing again with a code.                                          
• Choose a policy when pairing (--trust idle|<N>d|once|forever), change it
later (daisy trust  ...), and in the menu bar app.                      
• The peers file becomes structured, holding key, name, paired at, last seen
and policy; existing pairs migrate to the default.                          
• daisy peers and the menu bar show each Mac's policy and time remaining.
• Also offer rotating this Mac's own identity key, which makes every paired 
Mac pair again.                                                             
                                                                            
Revocation, forced and immediate:
- Remove trust for one Mac, several at once, or all of them: daisy forget <mac>..., daisy forget --all, and the same in the menu bar app.
- A revoked Mac is cut off at once: any live session with it ends, and in-memory trust from "just this once" and any open grace window are dropped.
- Revocation reaches the running app, and a running process must never write back a stale peer list that restores a revoked Mac. Today the running app saves its whole in-memory list when it pairs, which can undo a forget made from another terminal.

Tests: each policy expires exactly when it should; an active session keeps  
an idle-limit pin fresh but not a deadline; the grace window applies only   
after an unexpected drop, only for the same key, and only for 60 seconds; a 
peer claiming trust cannot override an expired local policy.                



BLOCKS
← ○ mn-9gq: Discover paired Macs with Bonjour ● P2
← ○ mn-e3p: Reconnect after sleep, wake and network changes ● P2
← ○ mn-075: Menu bar app that sets up and controls the connection ● P1

title: Share copied files
description: Required for the 1.0.0 release. Device-bound peer identity is its required trust prerequisite. Copying files in Finder and pasting on the peer. Transfer the contents with progress and cancellation, and put the received files on the pasteboard as file promises or from a temporary folder that is cleaned up. Handle folders and a size cap. A paired peer is trusted (docs/security-model.md: its behaviour is out of scope; it can already type on this system), so file transfer adds no new threat; the one file-specific concern is preserving macOS provenance: a file that carries com.apple.quarantine on the sender must keep it on the receiver so Gatekeeper still checks it.
design: Transport: Daisy's own Noise session, a second connection per bulk transfer so input stays unaffected; no rsync/SFTP/iroh/wormhole (each adds a second transport, identity layer or relay). Lazy: transfer on paste via file promises, not on every crossing. Atomic: write each file to a temp name beside its destination, fsync, copy extended attributes including com.apple.quarantine as sent, rename; build folders under a temp name and rename the top-level folder last. Compression: streaming zstd, adaptive level, applied before encryption, per-file compressor contexts, skip a file when its first block does not shrink; never compress input events. Stop reading at the declared size as a correctness check. Text/RTF clipboard items can use the same zstd step.
acceptance_criteria: Copied files and folders paste on the peer with progress, cancellation and clear failure reporting; no partially written file is ever visible; the quarantine attribute and other extended attributes survive the copy; deterministic tests plus a two-system check.
notes:
Fetch only what was offered: when control leaves a system its clipboard offer gets an ID; a peer may request only items in the current offer, by offer ID and item index, never by path. Any other request (unknown offer, stale offer, index out of range, path) is rejected and logged as a warning on the serving system. There is no listing or enumeration message. With requests bound to offers, a compromised member gains nothing beyond what the clipboard already gives it.
An offer ends, and its items stop being served, when the first of these happens: the destination says it is done with it; the destination has made no request against it for the idle TTL; a newer offer replaces it (the sender's clipboard changed); the session ends. Open question: 'done' should mean the destination's pasteboard no longer holds the promised files (its clipboard changed), not the first completed transfer, so pasting the same files into two folders still works. TTL value to decide.
Offer lifecycle (decided 2026-10-04, TTL 15 s): An offer of files goes to every connected group member, so any member can paste. Each destination holds a lease on the offer from the moment it arrives; any request or bytes still flowing refresh it, so long transfers are not cut off. A destination's lease ends when its clipboard no longer holds the promised files (it releases it) or after 15 s with no activity; at that point the destination also removes the promised files from its own clipboard so a late paste does nothing rather than fail. The offer ends, and the sender stops serving it, when every destination's lease has ended with no transfer in flight. A newer offer (sender's clipboard changed) supersedes it: transfers already running finish, new requests against the old offer are rejected and logged. A session ending ends that destination's lease. Members that connect after an offer is made do not receive it. Supersedes the earlier open question about the meaning of 'done'.
Device-bound identity is the trust prerequisite for sharing copied files. Completed Secure Enclave signing establishes that copying identity files cannot impersonate a paired system. Every future bulk-transfer connection must authenticate the same pinned Noise and device keys with a fresh device proof before accepting clipboard offers or file requests. This prerequisite is complete; file-transfer transport, offers, file promises, progress/cancellation, atomic writes and provenance preservation remain unimplemented.
Release gate: file transfer is required for 1.0.0, and device-bound identity was its required trust prerequisite. This supersedes the earlier optional/lowest-priority framing. Identity trust is complete; the 1.0.0 gate remains open until file transfer is implemented.

title: Daisy: many-to-many control across a group of systems with a shared layout
description:
Grow from one pair of systems into a group of systems that share input as one desk. Today Daisy is strictly two systems: the listener serves one connection at a time (src/main.rs accept loop awaits each session), each process has one peer on one edge (`--drive <side>`, a single `Side` in input.rs), and trust is pairwise only. The name Daisy comes from this idea: systems chained edge to edge.

What it looks like to the user: arrange any number of systems in a layout in the menu bar app, push the pointer off any screen edge and land on whichever system is there, as if it were one big desktop. Adding a system is pairing with any system already in the group.

Pre-planning only. Decompose into child issues and plan before building.
design:
Decisions made so far (2026-09-26):

1. Many-to-many, one controller per system. Any system can drive; a system is controlled by at most one other system at a time. HID control is enforced: the system whose physical keyboard/trackpad is in use holds control of the target, and a second driver cannot take a system already being controlled.

2. Shared layout in one global coordinate space. Every system's display(s) are rectangles with X/Y origin and size in a single global space. The layout is defined and edited dynamically in the control UX (menu bar app, mn-075) and distributed to every node, so each system knows where it sits by geometry. Edge crossing becomes "which rectangle does the pointer enter next", replacing the single `Side` model. Layout changes must be versioned so nodes agree on one layout; a stale layout must not route input.

3. Star topology with a coordinator, presented as a chain. The system in use coordinates and holds a direct session to every system in the group. When C joins through B (C connects to B, the system it knows), B introduces C and redirects it to the coordinator; C connects directly to A and is placed in the layout relative to B. To the user it looks like a daisy chain; on the wire it is a star. No hop re-injects input: a relaying system would have to re-capture injected events through its own event tap, which tangles pointer pinning and held-input release.

4. Transitive (introduced) trust. Accepted change to the security model: "I trust you and you trust them, so they inherit your trust." Mechanism: signed introductions. The introducer signs C's public key, trust policy and expiry; members accept it because they trust the introducer. Requirements:
   - Signed revocations propagate to every member; forgetting a system also revokes everything it introduced.
   - Stricter policy still wins: an introduced system's trust cannot outlive its introducer's.
   - A compromised member can admit a new system; docs/security-model.md must be rewritten to state this.
   - Short codes remain PAKE input only; never displayed for visual comparison.

5. Group stays awake; automatic re-establishment. While the group is active, every system holds a power assertion against idle system sleep (IOPMAssertion); displays may still dim. When control enters a system, declare user activity (IOPMAssertionDeclareUserActivity) to wake its display. Coordinate nap and wake across the group. If a system does sleep, it rejoins automatically once awake and unlocked, provided its trust is still inside its window and the trust keys have not been offline past the point where they can be refreshed. Unlock cannot be done across the group: the lock screen uses secure input and ignores posted events, so each system is unlocked locally (Touch ID); the coordinator shows which systems are locked. Do not change the user's lock settings. Overlaps mn-e3p (reconnect after sleep).

6. Latency is measured, not assumed. Add round-trip instrumentation (no clock sync needed) with p50/p99 histograms, surfaced as a stats command and in the app. Record in microseconds; network jitter dwarfs nanosecond resolution. Expected: tens of microseconds for capture/encrypt/send, ~100-300 us per wired gigabit hop, 1-5 ms per Wi-Fi hop with 10-50+ ms spikes. Wi-Fi hops, not processing, dominate.

Stretch goals (stay stretch even after building starts):
- Pass-through when direct fails: if C cannot reach the coordinator directly (subnet, firewall), B forwards opaque bytes. The Noise session stays end to end between coordinator and C, so B cannot read or inject. Costs one hop.
- Coordinator handoff: whichever system's hardware is in use becomes coordinator, seamlessly, since every node holds the layout. Only if it can be done without visible interruption.

Constraints from AGENTS.md: protocol::Message and InputEvent are encoded by variant position, so new messages are appended only. The event tap callback must stay nonblocking; layout lookups it needs are cached.

Decisions confirmed 2026-10-01 (supersede 3 where they differ):
- Topology: full mesh, not a star. Every system holds a direct Noise session to every other member; the system in use sends input straight to the system under the pointer. No coordinator, no handoff. Group capped at 8 systems (28 sessions). Pass-through stays a stretch goal.
- Joining: signed introductions (decision 4), with signed revocations and introduced trust bounded by the introducer's.
- Layout: one group layout of every display on every system (mn-pu5.1): free placement, no overlaps, light snap, crossing by direction of travel within reach. Agreed by version across the mesh.

description:

1. Enable Accessibility > Display > Pointer > Shake mouse pointer to locate on a macOS 26 following system.
2. Control it from a paired driving system.
3. Shake the physical mouse or trackpad pointer rapidly.
4. Observe whether Daisy enlarges the follower pointer and restores its configured size afterward.
